tldr: By introducing a refined actuator model capturing back-EMF coupling and magnetic saturation at high speeds, along with Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS) that smoothly guides velocity targets based on the current speed, the authors achieved world-record quadrupedal locomotion speeds of 11.65 m/s (approx. 42 km/h) outdoors and 13.2 m/s on a treadmill.
hero_caption: Overall reinforcement learning and real-world deployment pipeline of this study. By enforcing a torque-speed envelope in simulation that accounts for d-axis voltage coupling and magnetic saturation, the learned policy avoids issuing reckless commands that violate physical limits when deployed on the real robot.
overview:
When pushing quadrupedal robots toward their speed limits, actuators (motors) operate right at their physical boundaries and display strong nonlinearities. However, conventional reinforcement learning approaches have relied on simplified linear motor models or rough output clipping. Consequently, the simulated policy opportunistically exploits torques and speeds that cannot be realized in reality, causing a severe sim-to-real gap where the robot fails the moment it is deployed. In addition, training across a wide command range—from standing still to over 10 m/s—often causes training instability or drives the policy into overly conservative behaviors.

To address this, the authors built a refined actuator model incorporating d-axis voltage coupling and magnetic saturation, phenomena that become non-negligible at high rotational speeds. This accurately replicates the motor's actual torque-speed envelope (operating boundary) in simulation. Furthermore, they combined Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS), which dynamically bounds target updates relative to the robot's current speed, with a two-stage curriculum, creating a reinforcement learning framework that reliably learns across wide velocity ranges.

In experiments with their custom 36.5 kg quadruped robot "BlackPanther2 (BP2)", the robot achieved an astonishing top speed of 13.2 m/s on a treadmill and 11.65 m/s (41.95 km/h) during a 100 m outdoor concrete sprint. This sets a new world record for quadrupedal robot locomotion. The results clearly demonstrate that accurately modeling actuator physical constraints and providing realistic target updates are the key to unlocking extreme performance.
contributions: Built a refined actuator model explicitly accounting for d-axis voltage coupling and magnetic saturation, faithfully reproducing torque degradation at high speeds.
Proposed Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS), which dynamically restricts target velocity updates to the vicinity of the current speed, achieving stable learning across a wide command distribution.
Combined ACS with a two-stage curriculum learning strategy, smoothly scaling the policy from standstill to ultra-high speeds (12 m/s) without policy collapse.
Achieved world-record locomotion speeds of 13.2 m/s on a treadmill and 11.65 m/s in an outdoor 100 m sprint using the custom 36.5 kg quadruped BP2.

sections.heading: Challenging the Quadruped Speed Barrier: Why Breaking the Limit Is Hard
sections.summary: Under extreme dynamic running, motors operate near their physical limits, making nonlinear output boundaries and the sim-to-real gap major roadblocks. Handling a wide command range from zero to over 10 m/s in RL also causes severe training instability. This study proposes an integrated framework to solve both problems through refined motor modeling and adaptive command scheduling.
sections.details:
Quadrupedal locomotion control has shifted dramatically from traditional Model Predictive Control (MPC) to Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), successfully demonstrating acrobatic parkour and high-speed sprinting. While the hydraulic WildCat set a monumental milestone by reaching around 29 km/h (about 8 m/s), challenging and exceeding that speed limit using modern lightweight electric actuators has faced two fundamental obstacles.

First is the extreme modeling of actuators. When a robot reaches its velocity limits, joint motors operate directly on the boundary of their physical Motor Operating Region (MOR). In this ultra-high-speed regime, saturation effects and nonlinear torque-speed characteristics become dominant. However, prior learning methods either oversimplified motor characteristics or operated strictly within conservative margins far from the envelope boundary. As a result, policies in simulation exploited unrealistic power outputs, leading to a sim-to-real gap where the physical robot stalled or fell immediately upon deployment.

Second is the training instability stemming from wide command ranges. When forcing a single policy to cover everything from a standstill (0 m/s) to over 36 km/h (10+ m/s), large discrepancies between current and target speeds cause training to collapse, or lead to overly conservative policies that refuse to move out of fear of falling penalties.

The authors tackled these challenges by introducing a learning pipeline that integrates an actuator model capturing d-axis voltage coupling and magnetic saturation with Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS) that updates targets according to instantaneous robot speed. Deployed on the 36.5 kg real robot "BlackPanther2 (BP2)", this culminated in a new quadrupedal world record of 11.65 m/s outdoors.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Fast Locomotion and Prior Sim-to-Real Approaches
sections.summary: Control has progressed from early MPC based on simplified dynamics to DRL capable of handling full-body dynamics. For real-world transfer, black-box identification like actuator nets has been explored, but this work sets itself apart by focusing on a physics-based, low-dimensional model of motor operating boundaries.
sections.details:
### Evolution of High-Speed Quadruped Control
High-speed quadrupedal locomotion was historically dominated by MPC assuming Single Rigid Body Dynamics (SRBD). However, as speed increases, intense ground impact forces and underactuation become prominent, violating the assumptions of simplified models. While hydraulic robots like WildCat offered high power density, their actuation delay and system complexity have led to their replacement by high-bandwidth, lightweight electric actuators. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) utilizing massively parallel simulation emerged here as a powerful paradigm capable of naturally handling complex nonlinear contacts.

### Sim-to-Real Gaps and Actuator Handling
To transfer RL policies to physical robots, observation noise injection and Domain Randomization (DR) have been widely adopted. However, excessive randomization significantly degrades the upper bound of robot performance. To prevent non-physical behaviors, approaches such as neural network-based "actuator nets", frequency response measurements on physical hardware, and dynamic battery voltage modeling have been proposed.

Nevertheless, actuator nets lump multiple physical phenomena into a black box, hurting interpretability, and full-system identification is easily biased by coupled dynamics like contact forces. Furthermore, standard DC motor models in simulators like IsaacLab and conventional quasi-direct drive (QDD) constraints neglect the shrinkage of the operating region caused by d-axis voltage consumption at high speeds. While negligible at low-to-medium speeds, this modeling error causes a fatal discrepancy during sustained locomotion at physical limits.

sections.heading: A Refined Motor Model Carving Out the Limit and an Adaptive Curriculum Preventing Failure
sections.summary: The authors mathematically formulated magnetic saturation and the effect of d-axis back-EMF, which narrows available torque at high speeds, and applied it as a torque envelope in simulation. Furthermore, introducing ACS, which bounds velocity updates near current speed, alongside a two-stage curriculum, achieves stable RL training.
sections.details:
### III-A Refined Actuator Model with d-axis Voltage Coupling and Magnetic Saturation
In the rotor reference frame (dq-frame) widely used in motor control, current is decomposed into torque-producing q-axis current $i_q$ and flux-aligned d-axis current $i_d$. Typically, $i_d = 0$ control is employed to maximize efficiency. Conventional simplified models assumed that since $i_d = 0$, the d-axis voltage $v_d$ must also be zero, considering only the q-axis voltage $v_q$ against the DC bus voltage limit.

However, at high motor speeds, back-EMF and cross-coupling between axes induce a non-negligible $v_d$, even when $i_d = 0$. Because $v_d$ consumes a share of the available supply voltage $V_{\text{bus}}$ (with utilization factor $\gamma = 0.95$ in this work), the remaining voltage budget available for torque-generating $v_q$ drops. Consequently, the critical speed $\omega_c$ at which maximum torque can be sustained drops significantly. By rigorously solving $v_d^2 + v_q^2 \le (\gamma V_{\text{bus}})^2$, the authors derived an accurate torque-speed envelope from a quadratic inequality in motor speed $\omega_{\text{motor}}$ and output torque $\tau$.

In addition, torque constant degradation under large currents due to magnetic saturation was compensated using an empirical quadratic polynomial $\tau = \tau_c - \alpha \tau_c^2$, strictly constraining joint torques inside simulation.

### III-B Reinforcement Learning Framework and Two-Stage Curriculum
An asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture was employed. The Actor receives proprioception (joint positions/velocities, base angular velocity, gravity vector, previous actions) along with latent variables and estimates from a VAE (Variational Autoencoder) that estimates linear velocity, base height, and contact states from history. The Critic is additionally provided with privileged simulation states (ground-truth values).

The curriculum consists of two stages. Stage I (foundation) gradually widens target velocities from $[-1, 1]~\mathrm{m/s}$ to $[-2, 6]~\mathrm{m/s}$ to establish stable gaits. Stage II (extreme performance) rapidly extends the range up to $[-2, 12]~\mathrm{m/s}$. To suppress vibrations arising from actuator saturation at boundary limits, regularization reward weights are adaptively tuned.

### III-C Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS)
In ultra-high-speed running, how target velocity is supplied dictates policy survival. If targets are sampled uniformly at random, the gap between current and target speed causes either excessive acceleration attempts leading to falls, or a frozen policy that avoids moving to escape penalties. Fixed acceleration limits also exist, but they rely on manual tuning and fail to reflect velocity-dependent physical capabilities (differing acceleration capacity between standing starts and high-speed running).

Proposed ACS dynamically confines the next target velocity to a local neighborhood $[v_{\text{curr}} - \Delta v, v_{\text{curr}} + \Delta v]$ centered at the robot's current real speed $v_{\text{curr}}$ (set to $\Delta v = 1~\mathrm{m/s}$ in experiments). This naturally synchronizes command update rates with the robot's instantaneous dynamic capacity, enabling the policy to self-discover smooth acceleration profiles without tracking failure.

captions.F1: Comparison of torque-speed envelopes (first quadrant) across different motor modeling methods. Compared to the conventional $v_d = 0$ model (blue dashed) and unconstrained model (gray dash-dot), the proposed model (Ours, black dashed) accurately captures the substantial shrinkage of the operating region at high speeds due to d-axis voltage consumption.

sections.heading: Setting the World Record: Acceleration to 42 km/h and Ablation Studies
sections.summary: The policy was trained in parallel using IsaacGym on an RTX 4090 and deployed on the 36.5 kg BP2 robot. After validating the individual contributions in simulation, the robot demonstrated world-record speeds of 13.2 m/s on a treadmill and 11.65 m/s on outdoor concrete.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Ablation Baselines
IsaacGym was used for training, running 4096 parallel environments on a single RTX 4090 GPU. Joints used direct torque control reflecting high-stiffness passive spring dynamics, including rapid stiffness escalation near joint travel limits (soft contact modeling). The physical BP2 robot has a total mass of 36.5 kg, operates on a 60 V DC bus, and runs the high-level policy at 50 Hz and low-level motor loops at 1000 Hz.

To evaluate the proposed components, the following baselines were compared against Ours:
- Baseline: Rectangular envelope (no motor characteristics) + uniform random command sampling
- w/o torque–speed envelope: Motor envelope constraints removed
- Simplified DC model: Conventional DC motor model ignoring d-axis voltage
- Fixed acceleration scheduling: Fixed acceleration constraints (2–4 $\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
- Uniform command sampling: Uniform sampling across the entire speed range

### IV-B Simulation Experiments and Analysis
In Sim-to-Sim validation inside MuJoCo, the proposed method reached a top speed of 12.4 m/s, representing a 31.9% speed improvement over the Baseline (9.4 m/s). Looking at the stability metric $J_{\text{norm}}$, defined by base pitch and roll angular velocities, removing envelope constraints or reverting to uniform sampling caused notable metric degradation (severe attitude oscillation).

Policies trained without envelope constraints exploited unphysical torques in simulation; once hitting real physical limits, they suffered torque shortages and violent pitch oscillations (Fig. F3). Furthermore, while fixed acceleration constraints overfit to predetermined rates lacking flexibility, ACS naturally produced a state-dependent acceleration profile: smooth at low speeds, highly efficient in mid-range, and tapering near top speed to preserve stability (Fig. F4).

### IV-C Indoor Treadmill Experiment (13.2 m/s)
On an indoor custom treadmill, the robot recorded a top speed of 13.2 m/s (47.5 km/h) (Fig. F5). Safety overhead tethers were strictly for fall protection, providing zero weight support or forward assistance at top speed. Analysis of the gait cycle showed that ground impacts were absorbed as potential energy by joint compliance, released backward during the stance phase, and followed by a rapid forward swing, sustaining an impressive stride length and propulsion.

### IV-D Outdoor Sprint Experiment (11.65 m/s)
On an outdoor flat concrete surface, a 100 m sprint was conducted using an RTK positioning system. The robot completed the 100 m course in 11.67 seconds, reaching a peak speed of 11.65 m/s (41.95 km/h) (Fig. F6 (a)). Real-world hip motor operating trajectories (especially on rear legs) closely traced the envelope boundary predicted by simulation, confirming the high fidelity of the model.

captions.F3: Comparison of motor operating trajectories between the baseline without torque-speed envelope constraints (left) and the proposed method (right). The baseline fails by demanding torques in non-physical regions (outside the dashed curve), whereas the proposed method cleanly utilizes the space inside the envelope boundary.
captions.F4: Tracking comparison between command speed (solid blue) and actual speed (dashed orange) for fixed acceleration scheduling (left) versus the proposed ACS (right). ACS produces a smooth S-curve command matching the robot's instantaneous acceleration capability, avoiding tracking lag and excessive stress.
captions.F5: Snapshots from the indoor treadmill experiment. (a)–(d) show one gait cycle of the right hind leg at peak speed (touchdown, energy storage, push-off, high-speed swing), and (e) displays the recorded peak speed of 13.2 m/s.

sections.heading: Governing Factors of the Speed Limit and Future Architectural Directions
sections.summary: Actuator boundaries dictate top speed, with current performance bottlenecked by load concentration on hip motors. Future improvements will center on flux-weakening control and distributing joint loads via waist joints and trajectory optimization.
sections.details:
Experimental outcomes clearly highlight that quadrupedal locomotion limits are fundamentally dictated by actuator Motor Operating Regions (MOR). In simulation analyses, relaxing hip joint limits improved operating conditions at the knee joints, demonstrating strong inter-joint coupling. This indicates that even without altering hardware, electrically expanding the high-speed MOR via techniques such as flux-weakening control could yield higher top speeds and improved energy efficiency.

Concurrently, the current control policy revealed an excessive dependency on the output of hip actuators, particularly in the hind legs (Fig. F6 (b)). To resolve this load imbalance, the authors point to two future directions. First, using offline Trajectory Optimization (TO) with joint load equalization objectives as a prior for reinforcement learning. Second, mechanical design improvements, such as introducing an active actuated waist (spine flexion/extension) like a cheetah. Combining this with optimized mass distribution and link lengths would alleviate load concentration on single joints and help push speed limits even further.

captions.F6: Outdoor sprint experimental results. (a) Locomotion velocity profile measured by the RTK system, reaching a maximum speed of 11.65 m/s (41.95 km/h) at the 90.4 m mark. (b) Torque-speed trajectories across joint motors, showing that the hind-right hip (HR Hip) closely rides along the motor boundary (black dashed curve).

sections.heading: Conclusion: Accurately Knowing Physical Limits Makes Robots Run the Fastest
sections.summary: Combining high-fidelity actuator modeling with ACS substantially elevates the speed limits of quadruped robots. Achieving 11.65 m/s outdoors on BP2 proves the critical importance of accurately modeling physical boundaries.
sections.details:
This study presented a comprehensive control framework allowing quadrupedal robots to challenge their physical terminal velocities. High-fidelity actuator modeling capturing d-axis voltage coupling and magnetic saturation eliminated the high-speed sim-to-real gap, while a two-stage curriculum paired with Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS) prevented policy collapse across wide velocity commands.

The records of 11.65 m/s outdoors and 13.2 m/s indoors achieved on BP2 demonstrate the necessity of neither underestimating nor timidly backing away from physical limits, but rather teaching the exact boundaries to the simulator. These results establish a solid foundation for future research in extreme dynamics and high-agility control for legged robots.

takeaways: In sim-to-real for extreme performance, strictly formulating nonlinear motor operating limits (MOR) like d-axis voltage consumption into simulation is vastly more effective than blurring errors via domain randomization.

When training over wide velocity command ranges in RL, restricting target goals to a local neighborhood of current speed via Adaptive Command Scheduling (ACS) produces natural, stable acceleration profiles without fixed acceleration limits.

Because quadrupedal ultra-high-speed sprinting concentrates torque demands on the hind hip joints, adopting flux-weakening control or distributing loads across active waist joints will be key breakthroughs for future speed records.
limitations: Joint load during high-speed running is heavily skewed toward hip motors, leaving the output capacity of other joints, such as knees, underutilized.

Because the robot features a rigid base without a torso/waist joint, it lacks the ability to extend stride length through spinal flexion like a cheetah, leaving a mechanical limit where propulsion relies solely on leg joints.

A roughly 1.5 m/s gap remains between treadmill top speed (13.2 m/s) and outdoor flat ground speed (11.65 m/s), where outdoor surface friction, aerodynamic drag, and acceleration/deceleration runup distance continue to impose constraints.
